answer: Sontag argues that reality has come to seem more like its images than the reverse: people describe a real disaster as being 'like a movie', and the image becomes the standard that experience is measured against. Her example about the self is that we learn to see ourselves photographically. To think yourself attractive is to judge that you would look good in a photograph. She limits the claim to modern, industrialised, camera-saturated societies, where images are everywhere. She does not offer it as a universal truth about human perception.

Scarcity concerns how much of something there is: limited quantity, limited time, supply restricted by production or distribution. Exclusivity concerns who can get it: access depends on a qualification such as membership, invitation or insider status, as with Rue La La's members-only sales or a hidden restaurant. Berger insists that exclusivity is not only about money or celebrity. It can rest on knowledge, connections or behaviour, such as being a loyal customer or knowing the secret menu. Ordinary products can therefore create insider status and the social currency that comes with it.

By staking out the extreme of rigour and competition results, the first teacher gives up the families who want joy, balance and development of the whole child. They also commit to delivering winners. Those families are simply not their customers, and they must not try to win them back by blurring the promise. The general rule is Godin's positioning map: choose two axes that matter to the people you seek, find an empty extreme, and own it. Every choice of position deliberately excludes someone. Being for someone means not being for everyone.

The dividing line is whether you cannot get closer or are choosing not to. Telephoto is fine when physical access is impossible or would disturb the subject: wildlife, sport, candid moments you would destroy by approaching. Carroll warns against using it as a way to hang back and avoid engaging, because distance shows in the picture as detachment. Optically, a telephoto compresses space. It flattens perspective, so background and foreground appear closer together and elements stack into layers. Depth is squeezed rather than exaggerated, which you can use deliberately for graphic, flattened compositions.

The hot half works by switching off the internal critic. Judgement and generation interfere with each other: if you evaluate while you produce, you strangle ideas before they can lead anywhere. So you write fast and uncensored and aim for quantity, knowing most of it will be bad. For the cold half he prescribes distance. Put the work away, let time pass (overnight if possible), and come back to it as a detached, ruthless reader. Cut everything that does not earn its place and keep only what still holds up on sober rereading, often pinned up on the wall for testing.

Both pastel and muted colours sit toward the low-saturation core of Freeman's colour solid, which is organised by hue, saturation and brightness. They differ on the brightness (lightness) axis. Pastels are desaturated and high in brightness, near the upper, white end of the solid: pale, light, airy tints. Muted colours are desaturated at middle or lower brightness, pulled toward grey rather than white: subdued, dusky or greyed hues. So the two share low saturation and are separated by where they sit vertically, light versus mid-dark. [unsure]

In both cases the claim or disclaimer makes the reader ask what is not being said. 'Made with real cheese' implies that some of it, or the competition's, is not real. The asterisk signals a catch hidden in the small print. By trying to reassure or comply, the ad signals doubt and loses credibility. Sullivan blames the advertising industry itself for creating that suspicious audience: decades of hype, weasel words and fine-print tricks trained consumers to distrust ads and to decode every qualifier as evidence of deception.

Carroll is claiming that the meter's 'correct' exposure is only a technical average. The camera tries to render the scene as mid-grey, and that is not necessarily the right picture. Exposure is a creative decision about mood and emphasis, so the photographer decides what should be bright or dark. Later positions rest on this: deliberately under- or over-exposing, using exposure compensation (for example, for snow or dark scenes), high-key and low-key images, silhouettes against bright backgrounds, exposing for the highlights, and generally overriding the meter instead of trusting auto modes.

Sontag's claim is that photographs of suffering, made to arouse conscience, lose their force the more they are seen: 'Images transfix. Images anesthetize.' Repeated exposure makes horror familiar, less real and aesthetically consumable, and so erodes compassion. This happens regardless of the photographer's intention, because the dulling comes from the medium's reproducibility and its tendency to beautify, not from bad motives. The claim is not that such images never move anyone. A first encounter can be a revelation, like her own sight of the Belsen and Dachau photographs. Nor does she say photographs create a moral position. They can only reinforce one that already exists.

Feedback gathered this way rests entirely on each reviewer's own assumptions: their private understanding of the objectives, users and constraints, which nobody can probe or correct. The designer cannot ask clarifying questions, explain decisions or steer the critique toward the goals, so reactions drift toward personal preference and prescriptive changes. When the designer cannot attend, the source prescribes supplying the context in writing: the objectives, relevant personas and principles, and exactly what kind of feedback is wanted. It also advises a follow-up conversation so the designer can clarify and explore the reasoning behind comments. [unsure]

Ogilvy concludes that the products in the category are essentially indistinguishable. Manufacturers with nothing factual to say fall back on slogans, jingles and entertainment, so show business stands in for a real point of difference. The move transfers well because it needs only the published ads: anyone can audit a category's advertising for fact density and infer parity or a lack of product news. It is weak because it is an inference from absence. The missing facts could equally reflect creative fashion, agency habits, regulation or a timid client rather than true product sameness, and nothing in the ads verifies the conclusion.

Hopkins's regimes depend on the product and on how buyers judge it. Where goods are comparable and bought on value, such as staples or mail-order items, a stated low price is a strong argument and should be specific. Where price stands in for quality, as with luxury or prestige goods, a high price reassures and cutting it can hurt sales, because people judge worth by cost. Where the price would deter before desire is built, you sell the product's merits first and then justify the price, or hold it back. What decides which applies is whether buyers can compare values directly or rely on price as a signal. [unsure]

Bijapurkar tells the analyst to stop treating 'India' as a single market and always to specify which India: which consumer class, income segment, urban or rural setting, and region. 'The Indian consumer' is an average that describes almost nobody. This matters beyond definition because aggregate figures blend radically different consumers, such as a thin affluent top, a large aspiring middle and a vast low-income base. Market sizes, growth rates and strategies built on the average therefore misestimate demand, misprice products and target a fictional customer. The unit of analysis decides the strategy.

At the presentation you are selling the idea: the solution to the brief and the reasoning behind it, not a picture for the client to like or dislike. Airey advises presenting the rationale and showing the mark in real applications, often focusing on one strong option rather than a menu. If you get it wrong and present artwork for aesthetic approval, the discussion collapses into personal taste ('I don't like green'). You then pay in endless revision rounds and Frankenstein combinations of options, and you lose control of the outcome. [unsure]

No. For Samara, breaking the grid is legitimate only when it still communicates. Deconstructed or intuitive layouts must still create hierarchy, entry points and a readable sequence, and the unconventional structure has to serve the content and the reader. 'Intentionally unconventional' describes the designer's motive, not the result. A complaint that readers cannot navigate is exactly the test that matters. Until the layout shows that readers can find their way through the information, the job is unfinished. Freedom from the grid does not mean freedom from organisation.

Samara grants that grids dominate on screen for practical reasons: templated, database-driven and responsive systems need modular, consistent structure that can reflow across devices and hold constantly changing content, and predictable placement helps navigation and interaction. What he refuses to relax is the duty to communicate: clear hierarchy, legibility, intuitive navigation and a coherent visual logic. He also does not accept the technology as a reason for dull, formulaic layouts. Alternative structures remain possible and desirable on screen as long as users can still orient themselves and act. [unsure]

First, stop arguing and test. Key the samples and the advertising, trace what the sampled customers actually buy, and let the returns decide whether the cost pays. Hopkins says samples often cost more than the space yet are the cheapest selling tool, because the product sells itself. Second, do not scatter samples indiscriminately. Give them only to people who ask for them, via a coupon, after reading the ad, so they go to interested prospects who have already absorbed your story. That cuts waste and makes the cost traceable per customer.

Chapter 15 is 'Test Campaigns'. As I recall it, the 91 per cent figure is a proportion observed among the people reached, such as the share of users, inquirers or those canvassed who responded in a given way, cited to show how conclusive small-scale evidence can be. It is not the return on investment of a test campaign, meaning sales per dollar spent in a test town. It should not be quoted as a campaign return or profit figure. It is a descriptive percentage within one case, reported without the full context needed to generalise. [unsure]

Under the Law of the Shape (logotypes), the authors put legibility first because the name must be read and remembered, and a logotype exists to register the word in the mind. Decorative or 'expressive' faces that sacrifice readability weaken the brand. The cycle they describe is typographic fashion: expressive faces come in and go out of style, so a logotype chosen for its mood dates and must be redone, while plain legible type endures. They concede that a typeface does carry a mood, for example masculine versus feminine or strong versus delicate, and that some fit is desirable, but it must never cost readability. [unsure]

The two stages are research (brief and discovery) and pencil sketching. Research is for understanding the client, its audience, competitors and history, so that you are solving the right problem and have raw material for ideas. Sketching is for generating and exploring many ideas quickly and cheaply, without the software's pull toward polish and premature commitment, so thinking stays loose and iterative. Airey demonstrates this rather than just asserting it: his case studies show real sketchbook pages from himself and other designers, with dozens of rough thumbnails leading to the final marks.

In the Van Camp's case, the canvass of homes found that about 94 per cent of housewives baked their own beans and only around 6 per cent used canned beans at all. That changed the task completely. Fighting rival canned brands for a small slice made no sense. The advertising had to persuade women to stop baking beans at home. So the copy dwelt on the sixteen hours of home baking, the uneven, indigestible results, and the superiority of the factory-baked product, and offered samples to prove it.

The shared shape of the failure is that the caption asserts something the image cannot show on inspection: a date, an attribution, a claim of being 'first', an effect on sales, or legible copy. In each case the reproduction (small, cropped, low-resolution or missing the relevant text) does not contain the evidence, so the plate illustrates rather than proves. Two likely examples: a plate captioned as a campaign's first or a landmark execution whose date and source are not visible, and a plate whose captioned slogan or claim cannot be read in the reproduction. [unsure]

In the Law of Fellowship the authors say a dominant brand should not try to take the whole market. Competition builds the category, and a leader's share should top out around 50 per cent, or a little more. Elsewhere they cite with approval brands holding far higher shares, such as Intel's or Gatorade's dominance of 80 per cent or more, as proof of focus and category ownership. The reader is left with an unresolved tension. The 'ceiling' is a rule of thumb rather than a law, and the book offers no principle for when high share is a triumph and when it is a threat. [unsure]

Now: don't simply implement the list or argue by email. Thank the person, acknowledge the input, and ask to discuss it in the scheduled session, explaining that you want to understand the reasoning. In the session, treat each requested change as a symptom. Ask what problem or objective it is meant to address, and trace it back to the agreed goals, personas and principles. Turn prescriptive directions into critique ('this element doesn't achieve X because...') and explore alternatives. Next time, restate the purpose and the kind of feedback wanted when sending materials ahead.

Meta-popularity is popularity that feeds on itself: an image sells because it is known to sell. Publishers and wholesalers read success from order volumes and reproduce what is already circulating widely. The operation is triangular because producers (artists and publishers) do not reach consumers directly. They infer demand through distributors and dealers, whose orders and judgements relay and filter buyers' preferences. The same mechanism makes an image vulnerable to copying and piracy, and to fashion: once it circulates, rivals reproduce it cheaply, and when orders fall, dealers drop it quickly. [unsure]

On Carroll's account, cropping from far back is not the same picture. Getting physically close changes perspective and the relationships between subject and background, and it changes your involvement with the subject. Shooting from far away, whether through a zoom or by cropping later, keeps the distant, flattened perspective and a detached feel. You also discard pixels, so resolution and quality suffer. His reason is that you should 'zoom with your feet': move closer, engage, and compose in camera, because where you stand shapes the photograph.

Run Airey's practical tests. Print it in one colour and in black and white. Scale it down to very small sizes (for example, favicon or roughly one inch) and check it holds. Reverse it out on dark backgrounds. Mock it up on real applications such as stationery, signage and web. Do a trademark and similarity search against existing marks. Determinate results: whether it survives mono reproduction, reduction and reversal, and whether direct conflicts appear in the search. Judgements: whether it is simple, relevant, distinctive, memorable, adaptable in spirit and timeless.

Neither has it fully right. Under Connect, Google's ABCDs advise humanising the ad by featuring people, especially faces and people using the product. They also advise focusing on the product and showing it clearly, and for action objectives they stress early branding and a clear call to action (Direct). So cutting people entirely goes against the humanising guidance, and a cast-led story that sidelines the product and the action ask misses the product-focus and Direct guidance. The source supports people using and demonstrating the product, with branding early and a clear CTA.

Godin's explanation is loss aversion and ownership. Once the glasses are in your hands, keeping them is the default and sending them back feels like giving something up. The decision flips from 'should I spend money?' to 'do I want to lose these?', and people hate losing what they already have (the endowment effect). The honest status of the result is anecdotal. It is a reported story with no controlled comparison, sample size or independent data, told to illustrate a principle rather than to prove it. [unsure]

The Jenson & Nicholson poster, built around the line 'Whenever you see colour, think of us', contains colour itself: a vivid, colourful scene or image with the brand name and slogan, with no can, no pack and no painter. It makes an associative, category-ownership claim rather than a product-performance claim. It tries to attach the brand to the idea of colour everywhere, so that any colourful sight in the world becomes a reminder of J&N. That is a brand-memory strategy, not a demonstration.

The plate appears to show details the text omits: the rural, small-town setting with Aamir Khan in character, the Hindi-language headline, and especially the low-price, small-pack offer (the Rs 5 'chhota' bottle). The text treats the line mainly as a linguistic coup, turning 'thanda', the generic word for a cold drink, into Coca-Cola. The visual shows that the campaign was equally about affordability and rural distribution. That matters because the campaign's success cannot be credited to the slogan alone. Price and pack were integral. [unsure]

The claim is a counterfactual that cannot be tested. Those campaigns were not pre-tested, so we cannot know what a test would have shown. The list is chosen after the fact from the author's successes, so it suffers survivorship and selection bias, and it is self-serving. Campaigns that skipped testing and failed are absent. There is no data, no comparison and no independent check, only the author's assertion. So it illustrates his conviction and says little about whether pre-testing actually kills good work.

Desai's finding, in the matrimonial-advertisement analysis, is that vocabulary changes much faster than values. New words such as professional degrees, 'cosmopolitan' or 'broad-minded' replace old ones, but the underlying requirements (caste, community, fair complexion, family status, the demure homely bride) persist, often in updated terms. So lexical change is not evidence of modernisation. The format absorbs modern language to express continuity. The team is mistaking the surface for the structure, and would need to show that the underlying selection criteria changed. [unsure]

Freeman ranks exact alignment low. Viewers attend first to content, then to the stronger graphic elements such as dominant shapes, lines, contrast and colour. Precise alignments of edges and points tend to be noticed only subliminally, if at all. The ranking changes when the image is sparse, graphic or minimal, with little subject content competing. Then alignment becomes prominent, and near-misses read as errors, so they must either be exact or clearly avoided. Deliberate framing in geometric and architectural subjects also raises its importance. [unsure]

Chapter 2 is the Law of Contraction: a brand becomes stronger when you narrow its focus. The diagnostic asks what made the leader a leader. It was narrow focus on one category, not its line extensions. Its launch into three adjacent categories is a sign of the leader weakening itself, surviving on strength already built, not a recipe for success. The founder is copying the effect and ignoring the cause. The correction is not to imitate the leader but to be different and narrower: own a single word or category, ideally as the first brand in a new one.

WCAG's understanding material for contrast says an outline around letters can be treated either as part of the text or as its background, depending on how it functions. A thick outline defines the visible letter shape, so its colour counts as the text colour and is measured against the surrounding background. A thin outline or halo acts as a separating edge, so the fill is the text and the outline serves as the background it is measured against. The mechanism is perceptual. What the eye takes as the letterform, and therefore what must contrast, depends on the outline's weight relative to the stroke. [unsure]

Hopkins holds that prevention is a weak appeal. People will do little to prevent troubles but will pay to cure them or to gain a positive benefit, so ads should promise gains such as beauty, health or pleasure rather than warn of ills. His evidence is traced results from keyed tests. Positive, happy appeals consistently outperformed negative, fear-based ones. His Pepsodent example sold whiter, film-free teeth, a beauty benefit, rather than decay prevention, and it succeeded where preventive toothpaste appeals had failed.

Godin's empathy principle is that other people don't know what you know, don't want what you want and don't believe what you believe, and that's okay. The closing clause means you may not treat them as wrong, ignorant or in need of correction. The demand shifts from persuading them to adopt your view to understanding and serving theirs. His strongest formulation of the consequence is that it is never the customer's fault. If your offer doesn't resonate, you chose the wrong people or the wrong story. The market is right about what it wants, and your job is to change, not to scold. [unsure]

As a student, Carroll judged a celebrated photographer's work (I believe William Eggleston) picture by picture, found individual frames banal and ordinary, and dismissed them. The error was using the single image as the unit of judgement. The correct unit is the body of work: the series, its sequence and consistent vision, where meaning builds across pictures. The evidence is personal anecdote, a confession offered to illustrate the point, not an argument or data, so it shows the principle rather than demonstrating it. [unsure]

The chapter says the choice is not a technical rule. Both bright-field and dark-field lighting describe glass correctly, by giving its edges dark lines on a light ground or light lines on a dark ground. Which to use depends on the subject, the background, the mood and the photographer's taste and purpose. Its real aim was to teach the underlying principle: controlling the edges of glass through the family of angles, meaning where the light sources sit relative to the angles that produce edge reflections. Once you understand that, you can build either look and choose for yourself.

Dwyer and Patel show darshan as a reciprocal devotional exchange: seeing and being seen by the deity. Hindi cinema and popular prints borrow its frontality to confer sacred or heroic aura on stars and gods, but its force comes from the devotional framework and recognised iconography around it, not from pose alone. So a product held still, frontal and looking out can borrow some iconic authority. Without an established reverence or narrative it may read as kitsch, as parody, or even as irreverent use of a sacred mode. The proposal's claim that the pose automatically confers authority overreaches what the source establishes.

It is not a contradiction. The two statements are at different levels. One describes the credit photographs receive: people treat them as traces stencilled off the real, more innocent and more trustworthy than paintings. The other is Sontag's critical claim that they are nevertheless selective, framed interpretations. The gap between belief and fact is her subject: the photograph's authority is partly an illusion that gives it power. When using the source, separate what she reports about cultural attitudes from what she asserts herself, and treat her aphoristic essays as argument, not empirical findings.

A trigger must be linked to the desired behaviour and present in the environment where that behaviour happens. Being vivid and often thought of is not enough, and a message can even trigger the wrong behaviour. Anti-drug ads that showed drug use reminded viewers of drugs and implied that everyone uses them. Berger's contrasting case is the healthy-eating study in university dining halls. 'Each and every dining hall tray needs five fruits and veggies a day' worked better than a generic healthy slogan, because the tray, a cue present at the moment of choice, triggered the behaviour.

Airey argues that the brief forces the client to think clearly about goals, audience, positioning and constraints. Writing it creates a shared, agreed understanding and gives you an objective standard to judge designs against, so feedback refers to the agreed objectives rather than to taste. It also protects both parties from scope and direction changes. What it does not let you do is skip further research and conversation with the client, or treat the brief as a guarantee that the solution will be accepted. It is the start of understanding, not a substitute for it. [unsure]

Samara expects the inversion to work because images already have their own internal structure: lines, masses, axes, directional movement and tonal areas. That structure can generate a layout as validly as an imposed column grid, and it ties text and picture together organically. The two directions are to let typography and other elements echo, align with or extend the image's internal geometry (congruence), or to set them against it in deliberate contrast and opposition, creating tension. [unsure]

In chapter 2, Ogilvy says to repeat a winning ad until it stops selling: you are advertising to a moving parade, not a standing army, and good ads can run for years. In this chapter he notes that readership or response on repeated insertion declines, or treats repetition more cautiously, which pulls against 'repeat indefinitely'. This is not a disagreement between sources because both claims come from the same author in the same book. It is an internal tension, most likely resolved by context: different media, response measures or evidence bases, which the reader must reconcile. [unsure]

The sidebar treats the refusal as a sign that the participants don't see the critique as valuable or as their responsibility. It reveals a problem of engagement and buy-in, often driven by seniority and power dynamics, not a problem of electronics. A facilitator cannot win by personal authority over senior people. Instead, establish ground rules the group agrees to up front, explain the purpose and value of the session, and make the norms the team's own, so everyone enforces them. Keep sessions focused and short so full attention is a reasonable ask. [unsure]

Jain's retouching case shows that production conventions in the calendar-art trade persist because they are embedded in networks of craft skill, dealer expectation and buyer acceptance, not because anyone can state their function. It licenses the conclusion that 'we've always done it' does not show the step is useless. Unexamined practices can carry tacit functions that the market recognises. You would still need to establish what, if anything, the step does for this audience and this output, for example by testing removal and checking acceptance or quality. The case cannot prove that your step is necessary. [unsure]

The book treats the bottle and the label as different surfaces. The glass needs a direct reflection within its family of angles to show a describing highlight. The paper label shows a direct-reflection sheen whenever the same light is placed in its family of angles too. The options are: narrow the light (strip light) and position it so the highlight falls on the glass beside the label; flag or mask part of the source so it doesn't reach the label's angles; light the label separately from outside its family; or composite two exposures. It rules out a polarizer as the fix, because it would also kill the glass highlight that makes the bottle look premium. [unsure]

Desai argues that status is relational. A signal of wealth or modernity exists only when others see and read it, so owners make sure it is visible, sometimes at the expense of use. His exemplary case is keeping the brand label stitched on the sleeve of a new suit, or leaving the plastic covers on car seats and appliances, so that newness and brand are displayed and never lost. Value lies in the recognition by others, not in the object itself. [unsure]

In the cycle, a boom follows liberalisation or a new category launch. Early sales grow fast, companies extrapolate them into huge market forecasts (the '300 million middle class' story), and then growth stalls and disappointment sets in. Bijapurkar's distinction is between one-time pent-up demand, drawn from a thin, already affluent top layer finally able to buy, and sustainable, broad-based demand from rising incomes across the larger segments below. Early growth is stock-filling at the top, not a trend. Once that pool saturates, and without products priced for the next strata, growth stagnates. That is what makes it a mechanism.

Estimate-talk-estimate is a Delphi-like procedure. First, each participant makes an independent private estimate, which preserves independence and prevents anchoring on the first speaker, social pressure and informational cascades. Then the group discusses, with members sharing their estimates and reasoning, which pools information and exposes different perspectives. Finally, each member makes a new private estimate, and these are averaged. This lets people update on the information without conforming to dominant voices or group polarisation, and averaging independent judgements reduces noise.

For Sontag, a photograph on its own is mute and ambiguous. Its meaning depends on the words and context around it, so assessing the image alone misses how the headline will direct its reading. The caption is 'the missing voice'. Assessing the pair does not fix the deeper problem. Even an accurate caption is only one interpretation, and a limiting one. The meaning still shifts with where, when and by whom the image is seen, and it changes over time and across venues. The image can also outlast or overpower its caption.

Freeman considers two moments worth the frame. One is the peak of the ball's arc, where it momentarily stops and upward motion turns to downward, giving a sharp and balanced moment. The other is the contact moment, when the ball is caught or leaves the hand. Anything between them is an arbitrary slice. He relates this to his earlier discussion of timing and the decisive moment, where peak action is a predictable instant of stasis you can anticipate rather than react to. [unsure]

Hopkins reports keyed returns showing that the identical advertisement drew inquiries at very different costs per reply. His examples range from a few cents to many times more, and he attributes the difference to variables such as the headline, the medium or publication, and the season or position, not to the copy's body. The passage is evidentially stronger than most of the book because the ad was held constant and responses were traced by key. That is a quasi-controlled comparison with measured outcomes, rather than an anecdote or assertion. [unsure]

What can be said is that Google reports ads aligned with the ABCDs showing around a 30 per cent lift in short-term sales likelihood (or a similar metric), based on analysis it conducted or commissioned, for example with Kantar. What cannot be said is that the figure was independently verified or peer-reviewed, that it shows causation rather than correlation between creative traits and outcomes, or that it generalises to your category. The publisher also sells the advertising inventory, and the methodology and sample are not fully disclosed.

Instead of broadening the brand, the authors offer two routes. One is to grow the category, which enlarges the market the narrow brand already owns. The other is to launch a separate second brand, with its own name and word, for each new market. The mechanism is that a brand's power is inversely proportional to its scope. Narrow focus keeps its word in the mind, and when the category expands, the brand that owns it expands with it. Extending the name would dilute the word and weaken the core. [unsure]

Desai argues that free coriander is not about price. It is a cultural ritual of the transaction. Getting a little something extra is part of what makes an exchange feel fair and personal: it enacts the relationship with the vendor and the shopper's sense of having struck a good deal. It is value-seeking behaviour that persists across income levels, not economic need, so it tells you little about price elasticity. His confidence is interpretive. It is an essayist's cultural reading from observation, not a measured finding. [unsure]

Place a small test light, or a point source, near the lens and move it around the subject while watching from the camera position. Note each position where the light reflects directly in the surface and each where it stops. The boundary positions mark the edges of the family of angles, which you can mark with tape or stands. The inversion is to swap light and viewpoint: put the light where the camera is and look from the subject's side, or think of the camera as the light source. Because light paths are reversible, hot spots then become easy to see. [unsure]

The authors say publicity builds brands and advertising maintains them. A leader should see its advertising budget as defensive: it maintains and protects a position already won through publicity, rather than creating it. The budget buys insurance, protection against competitors attacking the leadership position. They use an insurance analogy, treating advertising as the premium the leader pays to keep its brand on top. I cannot quote the exact wording with confidence. [unsure]

Berger's objection is that money crowds out the real motive for sharing. People share because it makes them look good (social currency) and helps others. Paying them turns a social act into a commercial one: it makes referrers look like shills, undermines the intrinsic motivation, and sharing stops once the payment does. Instead he proposes leveraging social currency: make people feel like insiders, give them something remarkable to talk about, use game mechanics and status, and create exclusivity. Customers then share because it enhances their self-image.

First, more questions don't produce independent assessments. The halo effect bleeds an overall impression across items, and long forms invite fatigue and inconsistency (occasion noise). Second, unless each item is anchored on a shared scale with a common frame of reference, more items add more room for level noise and pattern noise. The book favours a small set of well-defined mediating assessments, about five or six, rated on relative scales. Third, extra raters reduce noise only if their judgements are independent and aggregated. If they discuss first, cascades and group polarisation can amplify error rather than cancel it.

Pandey rejects research as the judge of creative work: pre-testing ads, focus-group verdicts and scoring that decide whether an idea lives. He keeps research as input for understanding consumers and markets. He puts in its place deep immersion in real Indian life, including observation, conversation, travel and everyday language, plus the gut instinct and experienced judgement of creative people and clients willing to trust ideas that feel true to how people actually live.

The visual pass has a null result because this source contains no images to analyse. Desai's book is a collection of text essays about Indian middle-class culture, with no reproduced advertisements, photographs or plates. It is not a gap in the analysis. It is a property of the source. The consequence is that any visual claims about the ads or objects he discusses cannot be supported from this book and must be checked against other sources that reproduce the material.

First, unanimity may reflect a lack of independence rather than clarity. If members hear each other before judging, informational and social cascades, deference to a senior member and group polarisation produce false consensus and inflated confidence. Second, the board may share a common bias: they agree with each other, low noise, but are systematically wrong. Agreement measures noise, not accuracy, and confidence is not validity. To distinguish them, collect independent private ratings before discussion (a noise audit) to see whether agreement survives, and compare decisions against later outcomes to detect bias.

The error equation (mean squared error = bias² + noise²) makes bias and noise equal contributors only for predictive or verifiable judgements with a true value, where errors in either direction are equally costly and error is scored by squared deviation. The book marks the boundary with asymmetric-cost cases, where overshooting and undershooting cost very different amounts. Its example is getting to the airport, where arriving late is far worse than arriving early. In such cases a deliberate bias can be sensible. Evaluative judgements with no true value also fall outside it.

Hopkins makes two objections. First, striking or unusual images attract the wrong people: the merely curious, not prospective buyers. An advertisement should single out and appeal only to those interested in what you sell, so attention for its own sake is waste. Second, pictures take expensive space and must earn it by selling. Art that is merely decorative or eccentric distracts from the salesmanship and lends frivolity to a serious appeal. Use pictures only when they help sell, and test them.

As I recall, Hopkins's 'great mistake' was a personal and career choice, not a failed campaign. It concerned how he spent his working life or handled a business arrangement, such as a financial or partnership decision he came to regret. That matters because, despite the title, the book does not report advertising failures in any systematic way. It is a success-oriented memoir, so the reader cannot use it to learn how often or why his methods failed. Survivorship bias shapes its lessons. [unsure]

On a flat subject such as a painting, avoiding glare requires lights outside the family of angles, which means placing them well off to the side at steep angles. Side lighting then falls off across the surface, making one side brighter than the other, so evenness and freedom from glare pull against each other. The solution that always works is to move the lights farther away. Greater distance reduces the relative difference in light-to-subject distance across the surface while keeping the light outside the family of angles. At the limit it becomes unusable: the lights need impractically large space and power, and exposure drops too far. [unsure]

Active listening means restating in your own words what you understood the other person to say, before responding or defending. The technique verifies understanding, not agreement: it confirms that what you heard matches what they meant and exposes misunderstandings early. When your restatement turns out to be wrong, the book singles out asking them to help you understand what you missed, for example 'Can you tell me more about that?' or 'What am I missing?'. The speaker then clarifies in their own terms instead of you guessing again. [unsure]

Even after the documents are written, circulated and reviewed, the team may not truly share an understanding of them or agree with them. People may have seen the personas, goals and principles without internalising or committing to them. Without that shared agreement, critique drifts back to personal preference ('I like', 'I don't like') and individual assumptions. Team members evaluate designs against their own unstated goals and relitigate decisions already made, instead of analysing the work against the agreed objectives.

The instruction limited to a readership is the assumption that readers enter a page at the top left and move left to right, top to bottom. That holds for readers of Latin and other left-to-right scripts, not for readers of Arabic, Hebrew or vertical East Asian layouts. The correct way to record it is as a conditional rule, scoped explicitly to left-to-right, Western reading conventions. It should not be stated as a universal law of navigation, and designs for other audiences need the entry point and flow mirrored or rethought. [unsure]

The two arrangements are, I believe, a subject lit from below on a translucent light table and a subject on a sheet of glass suspended above a separately lit background. The book treats the loss of a ground shadow as serious because the shadow anchors the object to a surface. Without it the object floats, and cues to its position, scale and contact with the ground disappear. The light table offers no way back, because the lit base wipes out any shadow. With the raised glass you can still reintroduce a shadow or reflection by lighting or dressing the background. [unsure]

Carroll's chain runs from intent to equipment. First decide what you want to say about the subject and its surroundings: include context, or isolate it. That decides the perspective and the relationship you want between subject and background, meaning how much space and depth, exaggerated or compressed. That in turn decides the focal length: wide to include and stretch depth, long to isolate and compress. Then you move your feet to fill the frame. Magnification, getting things bigger, is not the reason to choose a lens. [unsure]

The concession is that there is some truth to income thresholds: below certain levels, discretionary consumption is limited, and categories do take off as more households cross income levels. The objection is that Indian consumers buy many 'threshold' products (mobile phones, TVs, sachet shampoos) far below the predicted income, and adoption does not wait for per-capita averages. The diagnosis is that the theory assumes a single average consumer, a fixed price-performance offering and Western consumption sequences. It ignores income distribution, household pooling, and innovation that brings products down to what people can afford.

Bijapurkar requires that the segment be properly defined and deconstructed before the number is used. Which 'young professionals'? In which India: which cities, income classes, households? Is the label hiding a heterogeneous mix? Has the composition or size of the base changed so that the 12 per cent reflects a mix shift rather than behaviour change? Averages over a vague segment mislead. The closer parallel is her worked case on the loosely defined 'middle class' or 'youth' market, where an aggregate label concealed very different sub-segments and led to wrong sizing and targeting. [unsure]

From the history of modernist Swiss grid systems and the reactions against them (postmodern, deconstructivist and intuitive layout), Samara concludes that the grid and its breaking are not opposing ideologies. They are complementary tools. The choice between them should follow the content, the audience and the communication goal, not style or dogma. That conclusion is worth keeping because it is a working principle you can apply to any layout decision today. The history on its own only describes past movements, while the conclusion tells you how to decide.

Regional iconographic codes are the local conventions for how a deity or figure should look in different regions of India: attributes, dress, ornaments, colours, facial types, postures and associated symbols, such as distinctly South Indian versus Bengali or North Indian forms. They act as gatekeepers of acceptance. An image that departs from the local code is not recognised as the right or efficacious form and will not sell or be worshipped, so publishers and artists produce regional variants that match each market's expectations. [unsure]

Yes, flare is plausible. The book notes that flare in dark-field setups often shows up not as streaks or fogged corners but as overall veiling: lower contrast, a milky or flat look, and greyed blacks. Stray light from the bright background area outside the picture enters the lens and scatters. The remedy is to mask the background light so that it is no larger than needed, with black cards or flags cutting it to just outside the frame edges, and to use a lens shade. Then compare test frames for restored contrast.

Godin says the team is bored because it lives with the campaign every day. The market has barely noticed it. Internal fatigue is not audience fatigue. His memory claim is that people forget quickly and need many repeated exposures before a message even registers. Consistency and repetition build trust and recognition, so abandoning a campaign early throws that away. The stopping rule he actually supplies is to change when it stops working with the people you seek, not when you are tired of it. He gives no precise metric or threshold. [unsure]

The duplicates most likely come from the book's layout: pull quotes or callouts that repeat sentences from the body text were captured as ordinary text when the copy was digitised or extracted. They were found by a duplicate-sentence check during processing of the text. This matters beyond tidiness because duplicated sentences inflate apparent emphasis and frequency, can be double-counted as separate evidence in retrieval or quotation, and can misplace a quote's context. Analyses and citations need to deduplicate and trace each passage to its original location. [unsure]

The source records an advertiser answering the ban by substitution. For example, in surrogate advertising (liquor or tobacco brands advertising soda, music or other extensions), or by replacing a forbidden claim word with an image, coined term or euphemism, the brand keeps communicating the category. The mechanism is transfer: audiences already know the code, so the substitute inherits the forbidden word's meaning and the prohibition itself makes the allusion legible. This differs from a word wearing out, where meaning drains away through overuse. Here the meaning is preserved intact and simply rerouted around the ban. [unsure]

Pandey's governing principle is to speak to people in their own language and from their own lives: simple, human, rooted in everyday Indian and often Hindi idiom, aimed at the heart rather than the head. It comes from his upbringing in Jaipur, his family, cricket and his experience of ordinary Indians, which he contrasts with English-language advertising copied from the West. It is a practitioner's credo, a statement of belief drawn from experience and illustrated with his campaigns. It is not a tested or evidenced proposition. [unsure]

A keyed coupon loop measures immediate response per dollar. It cannot see failures that arrive through other channels or later: reputational, regulatory or product-level collapse, or buyers who do not repeat. The case in the book is Liquozone, the germicide 'cure' that Hopkins sold with enormous traced success through samples and coupons, until the patent-medicine exposés and pure-food legislation destroyed the business. Every keyed reading looked excellent right up until an external, non-measured factor ended it. [unsure]

The book is a memoir and anecdotal account. Reproducing the ads would need permissions from clients and rights-holders and adds cost, and the format relies on storytelling rather than illustration. As a result, the source can support claims about what Pandey says he intended, how the work came about and his reasoning. It cannot, by itself, verify what the executions actually looked like or claims about their visual craft. Those have to be checked against the ads themselves or other reproductions. [unsure]

The Amul topical hoarding is a fixed template with one variable. The Amul girl mascot (polka-dot dress, blue hair, simple cartoon illustration), the red-and-white look, the logo and the sign-off 'Amul: Utterly Butterly Delicious' stay constant. Only a punning Hinglish headline and a small scene about the week's news change. The inferred reason it works is that the constant elements make every execution instantly recognisable while the topical pun supplies freshness and talkability. Minimal illustration and copy mean it can be produced in a day or two, fast enough to ride current events.
